claims.claim_summary: ReAct outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while improving interpretability and trustworthiness
claims.claim_text_verbatim: We apply our approach, named ReAct, to a diverse set of language and decision making tasks and demonstrate its effectiveness over state-of-the-art baselines in addition to improved human interpretability and trustworthiness.

claims.label: partially_supported
claims.claim_summary: ReAct reduces hallucination and error propagation on HotpotQA and Fever
claims.claim_text_verbatim: Concretely, on question answering (HotpotQA) and fact veriﬁcation (Fever), ReAct overcomes prevalent issues of hallucination and error propagation in chain-of-thought reasoning by interacting with a simple Wikipedia API, and generating human-like task-solving trajectories that are more interpretable than baselines without reasoning traces.

claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: ReAct beats imitation and RL baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop
claims.claim_text_verbatim: Furthermore, on two interactive decision making benchmarks (ALFWorld and WebShop), ReAct outperforms imitation and reinforcement learning methods by an absolute success rate of 34% and 10% respectively, while being prompted with only one or two in-context examples.

claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: ReAct outperforms vanilla action models and competes with CoT on QA tasks
claims.claim_text_verbatim: For HotPotQA and Fever, with access to a Wikipedia API that the model can interact with, ReAct outperforms vanilla action generation models while being competitive with chain-of-thought reasoning (CoT) (Wei et al., 2022).

claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: Combining ReAct and CoT yields the highest overall task performance
claims.claim_text_verbatim: The best approach overall is a combination of ReAct and CoT that allows for the use of both internal knowledge and externally obtained information during reasoning.

claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: ReAct consistently outperforms action-only baselines in decision-making tasks
claims.claim_text_verbatim: We also demonstrate the importance of sparse, versatile reasoning in decision making by showing consistent advantages over controlled baselines with actions only.

claims.label: partially_supported
claims.claim_summary: ReAct generalizes well with few in-context examples, beating single-mode baselines
claims.claim_text_verbatim: C) Performant and robust: ReAct shows strong generalization to new task instances while learning solely from one to six in-context examples, consistently outperforming baselines with only reasoning or acting across different domains.

claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: ReAct beats CoT on Fever but slightly lags behind on HotpotQA
claims.claim_text_verbatim: On the other hand, ReAct outperforms CoT on Fever (60.9 vs. 56.3) and slightly lags behind CoT on HotpotQA (27.4 vs. 29.4).

claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: Hybrid ReAct and CoT-SC prompting strategies yield top performance
claims.claim_text_verbatim: Also shown in Table 1, the best prompting method on HotpotQA and Fever are ReAct →CoT-SC and CoT-SC →ReAct respectively.

claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: Finetuned ReAct scales efficiently, outperforming much larger prompted models
claims.claim_text_verbatim: However, when ﬁnetuned with just 3,000 examples, ReAct becomes the best method among the four, with PaLM-8B ﬁnetuned ReAct outperforming all PaLM-62B prompting methods, and PaLM-62B ﬁnetuned ReAct outperforming all 540B prompting methods.

claims.label: supported

claims.claim_text_verbatim: On ALFWorld, the best ReAct trial achieves an average success rate of 71%, signiﬁcantly outperforming the best Act (45%) and BUTLER (37%) trials.

claims.claim_text_verbatim: In fact, even the worse ReAct trial (48%) beats the best trial of both methods.

claims.claim_summary: ReAct improves WebShop success rate by 10% over prior best methods

claims.claim_text_verbatim: As can be seen in Table 3, ReAct substantially outperforms IM-style prompting (ReAct-IM) (71 vs. 53 overall success rate), with consistent advantages on ﬁve out of six tasks.
